The '''2010–11 Michigan Wolverines men's basketball team''' represented the [[University of Michigan]] during the [[2010–11 NCAA Division I men's basketball season]].  The team was coached by [[John Beilein]]. The team played its home games in [[Ann Arbor, Michigan]] at the [[Crisler Arena]], which has a capacity of 13,751, for the forty-fourth consecutive year.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mgoblue.com/facilities/article.aspx?id=28648|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080524172649/http://www.mgoblue.com/facilities/article.aspx?id=28648|archive-date=May 24, 2008|title=Crisler Arena|access-date=November 15, 2008|date=August 14, 2007|publisher=University of Michigan & Host Interactive}}</ref>  This season marked the team's ninety-fourth consecutive year as a member of the [[Big Ten Conference]].<ref name=MB07-8p190>{{cite book|title=2007-08 Men's Basketball Media Guide|publisher=University of Michigan|page=190|year=2007}}</ref>  The team witnessed the departure of its four tallest players and two leading scorers from the prior season.  The incoming class featured the sons of two former [[National Basketball Association]] players ([[Tim Hardaway]] and [[Tito Horford]]) and the younger brother of a current one ([[Al Horford]]).  Additionally [[Joe Dumars]]' son Jordan transferred to the team and [[Glenn Robinson]]'s son, [[Glenn Robinson III]] verbally committed to the class of 2012.  The season was marked by close losses against numerous highly ranked teams.

Although the team began with a 1–6 record in conference play, they rebounded to finish with a 9–9 conference mark.  This put them in a four-way tie for fourth and earned them a number four seed in the [[2011 Big Ten Conference men's basketball tournament]].  For the fifth consecutive year they won their first game in the tournament, but lost in the semifinals to eventual champion [[2010–11 Ohio State Buckeyes men's basketball team|Ohio State]].  They also earned a number eight seed in the [[2011 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament]], where they logged a record-setting performance in the first game, but lost in their second game (in the round of 32).

The team was [[captain (sports)|captained]] by [[Zack Novak]], who became one of the forty [[Academic All-American]] finalists for the second year in a row, and [[Stu Douglass]].  The team was also led by [[Darius Morris]] and [[Tim Hardaway Jr.]] who earned third team and honorable mention All-Big Ten recognition, respectively. Hardaway was one of two unanimous Big Ten All-Freshman selections. Hardaway set the school freshman single-season record for [[three-point shot]]s made and Morris set the school single-season record for [[assist (basketball)|assists]]. Hardaway was selected to the 2011 [[Collegeinsider.com]] Freshmen All-America team.

On NCAA Tournament selection Sunday, ''[[The Fab Five (film)|The Fab Five]]'' aired and comments it contained brought attention to issues of race in sports and education and the [[Duke Blue Devils men's basketball|Duke]]–Michigan rivalry.  Past Duke and Michigan players traded barbs in leading national newspapers.  The teams met in the 2011 NCAA tournament the following week with Duke prevailing.

It also marked the ninth straight time that John Beilein led a team victory in its first game of a postseason tournament (5 NCAA and 4 [[National Invitation Tournament|NIT]]).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mgoblue.com/sports/m-baskbl/recaps/031811aaq.html|title=Postgame Notes: Michigan 75, Tennessee 45|access-date=March 18, 2011|date=March 18, 2011|publisher=[[CBS Interactive]]|work=MGoBlue|author=Wyrot, Tom|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110401040823/http://www.mgoblue.com/sports/m-baskbl/recaps/031811aaq.html|archive-date=April 1, 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In the second round of the tournament, the team opposed [[2010–11 Duke Blue Devils men's basketball team|Duke]]. Duke prevailed 73–71.  In the game, Morris set a new Michigan single-season assist record with a total of 235.<ref name="CBS Interactive"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=310790150|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306234937/http://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=310790150|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 6, 2019|title=Blue Devils outlast Michigan to reach Sweet 16, give Mike Krzyzewski win No. 900|access-date=March 20, 2011|date=March 20, 2011|publisher=[[ESPN]]}}</ref>  The matchup came in the week following the media storm that erupted as a result of comments made in the [[ESPN films]] ''[[30 for 30]]'' documentary ''[[The Fab Five (film)|The Fab Five]]'' by [[Fab Five (University of Michigan)|Fab Five]] member and former Wolverine [[Jalen Rose]].  The controversy spread to ''[[The Washington Post]]'' where [[columnist]] Jason Reid noted that the film went out of its way to present inappropriate racial commentary when it described [[Duke Blue Devils men's basketball|Duke basketball]] [[head coach]] [[Mike Krzyzewski]] recruits as [[Uncle Tom]]s.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/jalen-roses-comments-on-race-in-espn-documentary-are-misguided/2011/03/12/ABFHbLS_story.html|title=Jalen Rose's comments on race in ESPN documentary are misguided|access-date=March 17, 2011|date=March 13, 2011|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|author=Reid, Jason}}</ref>  Among those critical of the racial commentary was Duke player [[Grant Hill]] who was cited in an [[Associated Press]] story that ran in major national media outlets.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2011/mar/16/hill-takes-issue-with-rose-in-fab-five-flap/|title=Hill Takes Issue In Fab Five Flap|access-date=June 8, 2011|date=March 16, 2011|work=[[The Washington Times]]}}</ref>  In fact, Hill blogged on ''[[The New York Times]]'' with a response.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://thequad.blogs.nytimes.com/2011/03/16/grant-hills-response-to-jalen-rose/|title=Grant Hill's Response to Jalen Rose|access-date=March 17, 2011|date=March 16, 2011|work=[[The New York Times]]|author=Hill, Grant| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110317093816/http://thequad.blogs.nytimes.com/2011/03/16/grant-hills-response-to-jalen-rose/| archive-date= March 17, 2011 | url-status= live}}</ref> Hill's response was the most emailed story in ''The New York Times'' and was shared on [[Facebook]] by nearly a 100,000 people within its first few days.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/aponline/2011/03/18/sports/AP-US-Uncle-Toms.html?|title='Uncle Tom' Remark Exposes Pain in Black Community|access-date=March 19, 2011|date=March 18, 2011|work=The New York Times}}</ref>
